items.title: George Benson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: The interviewer mentions 'Don Sebesky sweetening' in the context of George Benson's CTI era, but George Benson does not mention Don Sebesky in his response or the rest of the transcript.

One of the things that people are going to look at throughout history, they’re going to look at George Benson starting – making his recording career as – with organ, with Jack McDuff, working in the format that was really gaining popularity as soul jazz in the early ’60s, and then crossing over to more of an r-and-b format in the late ’60s with Verve, and then moving into the CTI – A&M, the CTI era of George Benson with all the real – the Don Sebesky sweetening and all of that. Definitely. Let me tell you. I talked about a young man named Larry Smith who took me to his house. I drove him home from a gig. We were both kids, 17 years old. He said – he offered me a cup of coffee, so I’d stay awake, driving back home. Then he played Charlie Parker. I said, that’s it. That’s the way music should be. That is the epitome of music. As far as I’m concerned, that’s what I think music should be. I played that record, Just Friends, because it happened to be on the jukeboxes all over the city. So…
